clue.text: Person who's temperamental and prudish, an academic going to North America

parts.note: prudish means prim, primly proper
taken as written
a don is a university lecturer

explanation.surface: A strait-laced, moody lecturer heads off to the United States.
explanation.walkthrough: 'going to' simply joins the academic to the abbreviations that follow.
explanation.definitionFit: A prima donna, originally the leading opera soprano, is now any vain, temperamental performer or colleague.

clue.text: Turbulence may make waves

parts.note: read literally, rough water tosses a vessel about; read as an idiom, to make waves is to stir up trouble, and the phrase meaning both is the answer

explanation.walkthrough: The clue works two ways at once: storms literally toss a small craft, and 'make waves' is an idiom for causing a disturbance.
explanation.definitionFit: To cause trouble or upset a stable situation is idiomatically to destabilise a small vessel.

clue.text: Maps route meandering to Cheddar, perhaps

indicators.note: meandering means wandering about, so the letters of these two words wander into a new order

explanation.surface: A traveller plans a winding road trip to the Somerset village of Cheddar.
explanation.walkthrough: Cheddar looks like the Somerset village at the end of a route; it is the cheese. In Britain the word for a mousetrap also means cheap, ordinary cheese such as cheddar.
explanation.definitionFit: Mousetrap is British slang for plain, inferior cheese, cheddar being an example.

clue.text: Tramp? It's a kind of boat

definitions.meaning: a tramp is a vagrant who wanders from place to place
a fishing vessel that uses drift nets

explanation.surface: A vagrant is compared to a vessel.
explanation.definitionFit: A vagrant who wanders aimlessly is a drifter, and a herring boat using drift nets is also so called.

clue.text: Young men were forced into this race to the office

definitions.text: Young men were forced into this

parts.note: the Grand National is Britain's famous steeplechase horse race, often called simply the National
an office is a church service, as in the divine office

explanation.surface: Young men were pushed into a scramble for desk jobs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'race to the office' suggests a dash to work; the Grand National is a British horse race, and 'office' is a religious service. 'to' just joins them.
explanation.definitionFit: Compulsory military conscription in Britain until 1960 drafted young men for a fixed period.

clue.text: A row about the Spanish studio

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the word for a row goes around the Spanish article

parts.note: a tier is a row, as of seats
el is Spanish for the

explanation.surface: An argument breaks out over the Spanish artist's workshop.
explanation.walkthrough: 'row' looks like a quarrel, but here it is a line of seats. 'about' means the row goes around the Spanish word for 'the', giving TELIER.
explanation.definitionFit: An atelier is an artist's or designer's workshop, a synonym for a working studio.

clue.text: Have an argument in yard, perhaps

definitions.meaning: to argue or box in practice
a yard is a horizontal pole on a ship's mast, an example of a pole of that kind

explanation.surface: Someone quarrels out in the back garden.
explanation.definitionFit: Sparring is trading blows or words, and a ship's yard is a type of mast pole.

clue.text: Good set for experimental programme

parts.note: PI, short for pious, is crossword shorthand for good
a lot is a set or batch of items, as at an auction

explanation.surface: A promising set of conditions for a trial scheme.
explanation.definitionFit: A trial broadcast or scheme run to test it before a full launch is a pilot.

clue.text: Prince, perhaps, has two names

parts.note: Roy is a man's name
Al is a man's name, short for Albert or Alan

explanation.surface: A prince may carry a pair of first names.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads as royal naming habits; actually the two names are put side by side.
explanation.definitionFit: A prince is an example of a member of a monarch's family.

clue.text: Make aware of bill being reduced — strange

indicators.note: being reduced means cut short, so the word for a bill loses its tail

parts.note: an account is a bill to be paid
quaint means odd or strange in an old-fashioned way

explanation.surface: Someone is told about a bill cut down to an odd figure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'being reduced' cuts ACCOUNT down to AC, also the usual abbreviation for account.
explanation.definitionFit: To inform someone or make them familiar with something is to acquaint them with it.

clue.text: Contracted them by ruse for commission

parts.note: 'em is the shortened, contracted form of them
a ploy is a ruse or stratagem

explanation.surface: Someone took people on through trickery to get a job done.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Contracted' looks like signing a contract; it means shortened, giving 'EM.
explanation.definitionFit: To commission someone is to hire them, a synonym for taking them on to work.

clue.text: Witness attending trial

parts.note: at means present at, attending
a test is a trial

explanation.surface: Someone who sat in on the court case gives evidence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'trial' suggests a court case, but here it means a test.
explanation.definitionFit: To bear witness to something is to vouch for or certify it as true.

clue.text: Relation moving from the East

indicators.note: moving means the letters of the word shift into another order

explanation.surface: A family member relocates from Asia.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Relation' looks like a relative; it is just the anagram fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Oriental is an old adjective describing things of or originating in Asia.

clue.text: I cause cramp, spoiling international competition

indicators.note: spoiling means ruining, so the letters of these three words are spoilt into a new order

explanation.surface: An athlete confesses to bringing on muscle spasms that ruin a global contest.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface imagines a cramp ruining an event; 'spoiling' marks the anagram.
explanation.definitionFit: The America's Cup is a long-running international yachting trophy race, an example of a contest between nations.

clue.text: Bring up what is finally brought up

definitions.meaning: to bring up a child is to raise it
the hindmost part, as in the phrase about bringing up the back of a procession

explanation.surface: A parent raises whatever comes last.
explanation.definitionFit: To raise children is to rear them, and the back of a column is its rear.

clue.text: Marathon competitor, perhaps, given the bird

definitions.meaning: someone who runs on streets, as in a city marathon
a fast-running ground cuckoo of the American south-west

explanation.surface: An athlete in a long race gets jeered at.
explanation.walkthrough: 'given the bird' looks like the idiom for being booed; 'given' is just a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A runner who races on streets rather than a track, and the American desert cuckoo known for sprinting.

clue.text: He treats injured agent, not I

indicators.note: injured means damaged, so these letters are knocked into a new shape

explanation.surface: A medic tends a hurt spy but disclaims being the patient.
explanation.walkthrough: 'treats' suggests a doctor, but here it means negotiates.
explanation.definitionFit: To treat with someone is to negotiate, so one who negotiates or deals is a negotiant.

clue.text: Against including honour to European city said to be odious

indicators.note: including means holding within, so the word for against wraps round the next pieces

parts.note: con means against, as in pros and cons
the OM, Order of Merit, is a British honour
Paris is the French capital

explanation.surface: Opposing a decoration for a French city is thought hateful.
explanation.walkthrough: The proverb 'comparisons are odious' supplies the definition. 'to' is only a link joining the honour to the city.
explanation.definitionFit: The proverb holds that likening one thing to another gives offence, so such a likening is called odious.

clue.text: Destructive game, one requiring intelligence

parts.note: RU is rugby union, a game
I is the Roman numeral for one
nous is common sense or intelligence

explanation.surface: A ruinous sport that needs brains to play.
explanation.walkthrough: 'requiring' simply joins the pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Ruinous means causing ruin, a synonym for destructive.

clue.text: Insignificant place producing two presents

parts.note: now means at present, in time
here means present, in place

explanation.surface: A dull spot that yields a couple of gifts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'presents' looks like gifts; it means present in time and present in place.
explanation.definitionFit: Nowhere as a noun means an obscure, unimportant spot, as in 'the middle of nowhere'.

clue.text: Pluck heads off giant roses in temper

indicators.note: the heads of the four words are their opening letters, picked off and joined

explanation.surface: A gardener angrily snaps the flowers off huge roses.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pluck' looks like a verb for picking; it is the noun meaning courage.
explanation.definitionFit: Grit and pluck are both synonyms for courage and determination.

clue.text: More sturdy farm animals? That's right

parts.note: livestock or stock are farm animals
ie, id est, means that is

explanation.surface: Are farm animals more robust? Correct.
explanation.definitionFit: Stockier means thicker-set and more solid, a comparative for burlier.

clue.text: Sort of crush

definitions.meaning: ... means kind or character, as in a man of that ...
to tread or pound something flat

explanation.surface: A kind of squash.
explanation.definitionFit: A type or kind of person is their stamp, and to stamp is to tread down hard.

clue.text: Neat oarsman seen in lake

parts.note: neat is an old word for cattle, so an ox
the bow is the rower nearest the front of a boat

explanation.surface: A tidy rower is spotted on a lake.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Neat' looks like tidy; it is the old word for cattle. 'seen in' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: An oxbow lake is a curved lake left when a river meander is cut off, so the word can stand for such a lake.

clue.text: Jester employed by prince as well

parts.note: a wit is a joker or jester
Prince Hal is Shakespeare's young Henry V

explanation.surface: A fool hired by a prince as well.
explanation.walkthrough: 'employed by' is a link joining the jester to Prince Hal, whose companion Falstaff the surface recalls.
explanation.definitionFit: Withal is an archaic adverb meaning besides or in addition.

clue.text: White-haired person wearing nothing more than vestment

indicators.note: more than says the next pieces come beyond, after, the vestment

parts.note: an alb is a long white priest's vestment
in means wearing, as in dressed in
O is zero, nothing

explanation.surface: A pale-haired person wears nothing but a priestly robe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wearing nothing' paints a naked figure, but 'more than' just means the next pieces come after the vestment.
explanation.definitionFit: An albino lacks pigment, so has very pale hair and skin.

clue.text: Repetition of one note in reverie

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one

indicators.note: in places the note inside the word for reverie

parts.note: a trance is a dreamy state, a reverie
E is a musical note

explanation.surface: A single note repeats through a daydream.
explanation.definitionFit: Iterance is a rare word for repeating, synonymous with iteration.

clue.text: Piece of pop

definitions.meaning: to pop is British slang for to hock goods for a loan

explanation.surface: A bit of fizzy drink.
explanation.walkthrough: To 'pop' something in Britain is to pledge it at a pawnbroker's.
explanation.definitionFit: The lowest chessman, and pledging goods for cash, both carry this word.

clue.text: See pottery constructed as plate

indicators.note: constructed means built up, so these letters are assembled into a new arrangement

explanation.surface: Look at earthenware made into a dish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'plate' suggests crockery, matching 'pottery'; it is a printing plate.
explanation.definitionFit: A stereotype is a solid metal printing plate cast from a mould of set type.
